Care
kâr
n. (anxiety; also attentive charge; rendering Greek merimna and epimeleomai)
Old English caru, sorrow, anxiety. The KJV keeps both senses — care as burden and care as responsible attention.

Biblical Definition

Care means anxiety and also attentive charge. Peter commands the transfer: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” (1Pe 5:7) — one Greek word for the burden, another for God's attention. Christ names “the cares of this world” among the thorns that choke the word (Mat 13:22). Paul lists as his daily burden “the care of all the churches” (2Co 11:28), and Martha is cumbered about much serving and careful about many things (Luk 10:41).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines care as concern; anxiety; solicitude; noting some degree of pain in the mind, from apprehension of evil; and caution, a looking to, regard, attention, or heed, with a view to safety or protection.

expand to see more

CARE, n. Concern; anxiety; solicitude; noting some degree of pain in the mind, from apprehension of evil.

2. Caution; a looking to; regard; attention, or heed, with a view to safety or protection.

3. Charge or oversight, implying concern for safety and prosperity.

4. The object of care, or watchful regard and attention.

Key Scripture

1Pe 5:7 — "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you."

Mat 13:22 — "He also that received seed among the thorns is he that heareth the word; and the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word, and he becometh unfruitful."

2Co 11:28 — "Beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches."

Luk 10:41 — "And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things:"

Modern Corruption

Anxiety is treated as an unavoidable feature of responsibility, and Peter commands it be thrown off — while Paul carries the care of all the churches without contradiction.

expand to see more

1 Peter 5:7 uses two different Greek words in one sentence, and English hides the distinction: casting all your merimna upon him; for he melei for you. The first is anxious care — a divided, distracted mind. The second is attentive concern. The Christian is told to throw the first at God precisely because God has the second toward him. It is not a command to stop caring; it is a command to stop carrying.

Paul's line in 2 Corinthians 11:28 shows the difference in practice: beside those things that are without, that which cometh upon me daily, the care of all the churches. He was not anxious about them in Peter's sense — he had just listed shipwrecks and beatings without alarm — but he carried a genuine daily weight of responsibility. Responsibility and anxiety are not the same thing, and confusing them makes either duty impossible or worry inevitable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek merimna (G3308), anxious care; melei (G3199), it is a care to, of God's attention; epimeleomai (G1959), to take care of, as the Samaritan did.

expand to see more

Greek merimna (G3308) — anxiety, care; 1 Peter 5:7, Matthew 13:22, 2 Corinthians 11:28.

Greek melei (G3199) — it matters to, he careth; 1 Peter 5:7, Mark 4:38.

Greek epimeleomai (G1959) — to take care of; Luke 10:34-35, 1 Timothy 3:5.

Usage

"“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” — two different words in one sentence."

"“The cares of this world… choke the word” — anxiety as a thorn."

"“The care of all the churches” — responsibility carried without anxiety."
